In September 2013 the Chinese leader Xi Jinping, speaking at Nazarbayev University in Astana, Kazakhstan, proposed a "Silk Road Economic Belt" across Eurasia. It was the first public step of what became the Belt and Road Initiative.

A month later, in Indonesia, he added a "21st Century Maritime Silk Road" by sea. Together they became China's main plan for building infrastructure abroad: ports, railways, roads, power stations and pipelines, now with projects in more than 150 countries.

The choice of Kazakhstan was deliberate. Central Asia lies on the old overland routes of the Silk Road, and China already had big interests there, like the gas pipeline from Central Asia opened in 2009. Rail lines now carry freight trains from China across Kazakhstan to Europe.

Flagship projects elsewhere include the China Pakistan Economic Corridor, the railway from China to Laos, and the ports of Gwadar, Hambantota and Piraeus.

The initiative is argued over:

  • Supporters say it fills real gaps in roads, rail and power in poorer countries.
  • Critics point to debts, weak labour and environmental standards, and the military uses some ports could have. Claims of deliberate "debt-trap diplomacy" are widely disputed by researchers.

For Central Asia it has made China the main source of trade and investment, alongside Russia's older ties.
sum: In September 2013 the Chinese leader Xi Jinping, speaking at Nazarbayev University in Astana, Kazakhstan, proposed a "Silk Road Economic Belt" across Eurasia. It was the first public step of what became the Belt and Road Initiative.
